explain.say: Picture a car's rear-window demister: thin lines on the glass that warm up when you switch them on. That warmth is a resistor turning electrical energy into heat. On the board, a 12 volt battery drives current through a 4 ohm heater element. Let's find the current and the heat, step by step.

explain.say: Look at the heater element. Ohm's law says V equals I times R: the voltage across a resistor equals the current through it times its resistance. Turn it round and the current is V over R, so 12 volts over 4 ohms gives 3 amps. If the resistance were bigger, would the current go up or down?

explain.say: The ammeter, of course. Now the power, which is energy per second. P equals V times I, so 12 times 3 gives 36 watts. Two handy twins come from Ohm's law: I squared R, that is 9 times 4, and V squared over R, 144 over 4. All three give 36 watts. Which form would you use if you only knew the current and the resistance?

explain.say: I squared R, well done! Now a surprise: halve the resistance to 2 ohms and the current doubles to 6 amps, so the power doubles to 72 watts. Lower resistance means more heat at a fixed voltage. A real kettle works this way: 2 kilowatts on India's 230 volt supply draws about 8.7 amps through roughly 26 ohms. Challenge: check those numbers yourself.

faq.a: Ohm's law says the current through a resistor is proportional to the voltage across it: V equals I times R. Double the voltage and the current doubles, as long as the temperature stays the same.

faq.q: How do you connect an ammeter and a voltmeter?
faq.a: An ammeter goes in series, in the path of the current, and has almost zero resistance. A voltmeter goes in parallel, across the part, and has a very high resistance so it barely draws current.
asks: Is an ammeter in series or parallel?

faq.q: Why are there three formulas for power?
faq.a: P equals V times I is the definition. Replacing V with I times R gives I squared R, and replacing I with V over R gives V squared over R. Use whichever matches the two quantities you know.
asks: Which power formula should I use?

faq.q: Why does a resistor get hot?
faq.a: Moving charges keep bumping into the vibrating atoms of the material and hand them energy. That extra vibration is heat, and the effect is called Joule heating.
asks: Where does the electrical energy go in a resistor?

faq.q: What does the battery do in the circuit?
faq.a: The battery keeps a fixed voltage, 12 volts here, between its terminals. That push drives charge round the loop and supplies the energy the heater turns into heat.
asks: What does the 12 V source do?

facts: Georg Ohm published his law relating current and voltage in 1827.
One watt is one joule of energy transferred per second.
At a fixed voltage, the power in a resistor is V squared over R, so a lower resistance gives more heat.

quiz.say: A 6 ohm resistor carries 2 amps. What power does it turn into heat?
quiz.show: A 6 Ω resistor carries 2 A. What power does it dissipate?
quiz.why: P equals I squared R, so 2 squared times 6 is 4 times 6, which is 24 watts.

wrong.0: That is the voltage, 12 volts, from I times R, not the power.
wrong.2: That divides R by I, which is not a power formula.

quiz.say: Which meter must be connected in series with the part?
quiz.show: Which meter must be connected in series with the part?
quiz.why: An ammeter measures current, so the current has to pass through it.

wrong.1: A voltmeter goes across a part, in parallel.
wrong.2: A voltmeter in series would block the current with its huge resistance.
